title: What if paying bills turned into a psychological horror game?
summary: MANILA, Philippines – When the theme for the Filipino Horror Game Jam 2026 dropped, Angelo Barrera and the team at Mithika Games figured they’d end up making something with ghosts or local folklore.…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines – When the theme for the Filipino Horror Game Jam 2026 dropped, Angelo Barrera and the team at Mithika Games figured they’d end up making something with ghosts or local folklore. Then somebody pitched an idea as a half-joke: what about household bills?

Electric bills, rent, and grocery receipts don’t exactly sound like classic horror fare on paper. But as the team kept kicking the concept around, a much heavier question sank in: what if the real nightmare isn’t the bills themselves, but the person stuck paying them?

That spark became Breadwinner, a psychological horror title centered on a Filipino panganay (eldest child) trying to stretch a single paycheck across endless family expenses. Players spend their commute choosing what gets covered, from rent and electricity to meds for a parent or school fees for a younger sibling, before heading home to face the inevitable fallout of those choices.

Barrera, an eight-year industry veteran who has worked as a programmer, designer, and producer, mentioned that the idea took shape while looking for an angle on the jam’s “real-life horror” theme that wouldn’t get lost in the crowd.

Early on, they toyed with scenarios like floods, muggings, or stalkers. While scary, Barrera felt those situations lacked a universal, daily resonance. Someone might assume they’ll never get mugged, but having your monthly expenses outpace your bank balance is an anxiety almost everyone recognizes.

This went from family dynamics to the financial pressure on lower-income households, particularly what Barrera calls toxic sides of family culture. In many homes, the eldest breadwinner ends up supporting people far beyond their immediate self. A paycheck that could comfortably support one person suddenly has to keep an entire household afloat.

Making a game out of the bills

The pieces for Breadwinner didn’t start out in one game. Initially, the team had separate prototypes: one focusing on the walk home, another on a jeepney ride, and a third set entirely inside the family house. On day two of the game jam, Barrera decided to stitch them into a single narrative flow.

The result is a brief, focused journey through a single day in the protagonist’s shoes, where your financial choices directly alter the vibe and narrative progression. Instead of relying on jump scares or monsters, Breadwinner mines terror from that quiet, suffocating dread of watching your money run out while your responsibilities mount.

Honestly, the team wasn’t even sure if the game would hit when they turned it in. Barrera remembers wondering if they’d pushed the boundary too far, especially since it looked so different from standard horror jam entries.

Then streamers picked it up, and comment sections across Facebook, Instagram, YouTube, and TikTok blew up. Barrera said they were caught off guard by how quickly players picked up on tiny details and subtle themes they had tucked into the design.
Many players felt like the game was telling their exact life story, while others admitted the depiction of familial guilt hit way too close to home.

Mithika Games had initially worried the story might be too hyper-specific to the Philippines to resonate elsewhere. But surprisingly, Barrera started getting messages from players in Latin America saying the exact same dynamic exists in their culture.
“It’s Filipino-flavored,” he noted. The slang or local references might change depending on where you are, but the core story remains universally human.

That reaction highlights why Breadwinner lands so well outside its home region. While the panganay experience carries distinct local nuances, the grinding tension between family duties and a limited income isn’t bound by geography. The game doesn’t need to dilute its cultural identity for foreign audiences to understand the weight on the protagonist’s shoulders.
A two-week project gets a second life

Originally, Mithika Games viewed Breadwinner as a quick game jam project to finish, ship, and forget. Everyone on the team works a full-time job, so game dev is something they tackle on nights and weekends. The whole thing was thrown together in about two weeks without any master plan for a full release.

The overwhelming response flipped those plans on their head. Encouraged by the feedback, the team put together version 0.2, adding features and narrative beats that got cut from the original build. Barrera says they now see real potential to expand Breadwinner into a full-fledged narrative experience with richer gameplay mechanics.

Plans under consideration include expanding the commute route into a fully explorable neighborhood and giving players a closer look at the main character’s workplace. Barrera emphasized that the team is taking its time to flesh these ideas out properly rather than calling it done.

Voice acting has come up in discussions too, though the branching story makes voice recording tricky while the script is still evolving. Since players can choose between playing as a kuya (older brother) or ate (older sister), every narrative branch needs to be voiced twice.

A Steam launch is definitely on the radar, but Barrera feels the game isn’t meaty enough yet to ask people for money. They aren’t interested in rushing out a cash-grab just because they’ve caught a wave of hype. Instead, they’re looking at games like Until Then, another breakout Filipino narrative game, as a standard for storytelling depth and overall polish.

Barrera says the focus right now is quietly building out story paths, tweaking gameplay mechanics, and listening to community feedback. Mithika Games is also open to bringing in production partners to help bring the full project across the finish line.

Beyond Breadwinner, Mithika Games has diverse interests. Barrera pointed to Tata, a project created in collaboration with the Cultural Center of the Philippines to showcase regional arts and heritage. The studio intends to keep experimenting across genres while holding onto their quality standards.

On a personal level, Barrera dreams of making a sci-fi MMO centered on player choice and community dynamics. Growing up on StarCraft, Red Alert, and Dota, he always assumed his landmark project would be a massive commercial sci-fi game. A game about budgeting bills was never on his original radar.

Yet here they are, building on a project that started with a joke about monthly expenses. What began as a throwaway entry for a game jam has given Mithika Games a story worth telling at full scale. They’re still figuring out the exact contours of the expanded version but they are definitely on the right track.

At its heart, the game is relatable on so many levels from that monthly salary, a stack of bills, and a family depending on one person to make it all work. In more ways than one it really is scary stuff to think about.
